speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the years, public housing options for singles have gradually expanded ever since the introduction of the Single Singapore Citizen scheme in 1991.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, since the scheme’s inception almost 30 years ago, one key policy requirement has remained unchanged – that singles must be at least 35 years old to be eligible to purchase public housing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, recent headlines reporting record high HDB resale prices, suggest that something is amiss in public housing provision, even for couples.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This proposal would be a critical change, yet a continuation of the Government’s efforts over the years to expand HDB options for singles, while still allowing HDB to give priority to providing for families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we believe lowering the threshold for owning HDB flats to 28 years would go a long way towards HDB’s stated aims for Singapore’s public housing to be “inclusive” and to “reflect the diversity of our society”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The objective of today’s Adjournment Motion is two-fold: to ensure that the housing needs of not just singles, but those of all Singaporeans are met.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I move on to state my case on why singles should be allowed to apply for a BTO flat at an earlier age, I would like to touch on the most pressing issue in my view and, that is, housing supply.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In response to my Adjournment Motion last year on "Supporting Diverse Aspirations Through Rental Housing", Senior Minister of State Sim Ann shared that home ownership has been and will continue to be our key housing strategy for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Since this is the Government’s position, I hope that the Government can take steps to deliver on this strategy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that compared to last year, housing supply is set to increase by about 35% over the next two years, at about 23,000 BTO flats per year in 2022 and 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the HDB stated that it is prepared to launch up to 100,000 flats in total from 2021 to 2025, if needed, subject to prevailing demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These numbers, however, need to be put in context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if HDB decides to launch the whole 100,000 flats in total from 2021 to 2025, this implies that BTO supply falls 20% to about 18,400 flats in 2024 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while the average of 20,000 BTO flats between 2021 and 2025 is an increase, compared to an average of 17,000 flats between 2016 and 2020, this is still 13% below the average of 23,000 flats in 2011 to 2015, during the time when Mr Khaw Boon Wan was the Minister for National Development and sought to address the backlog in the supply of HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have already seen BTO application rates climbing steadily over the past decade to new highs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For 3-room and larger flats, this increased from 2.8 times in 2012 to 6.1 times in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, 2-room Flexi flats, whose buyers are more likely to be the elderly or singles, also saw application rates rise, albeit at a more moderate pace from 2.8 times in 2012 to 3.6 times in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is of greater concern is that despite the supposed ramp-up in supply this year, application rates have reached new record highs, suggesting that the level of demand-supply imbalance remains a critical concern.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is worrying, especially when we look at the recent August BTO exercise, where the overall application rates are seeing no signs of letting up, with that for 2-room Flexi flats at 5.5 times and that for 3-room and larger flats at 8.3 times.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I hope the Government will seriously prioritise its resources to support Singaporeans in achieving their home ownership aspirations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to reducing the BTO eligibility age to 28 for singles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By the age of 28, the average Singaporean male and female would have finished their tertiary studies and had some amount of time in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In that sense, they would have some chance to lead independent lives and steady their financial footing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared by Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh earlier this year, in the National Youth Council’s 2021 publication on the state of youths in Singapore, when it comes to aspirations or goals in life, the top choice selected by our youths was to maintain strong family relationships while the second choice was "to have a place of my own".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our proposal looks at reducing the BTO eligibility age to 28, and not that for the resale market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While opening the resale HDB market to singles below 35 is a possibility worth exploring, we think it is important to first enable singles to access the BTO market, to ensure that incremental demand is met through new supply and not through existing supply and via the currently buoyant HDB resale market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: No different from purchasing a resale HDB flat anyway.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Affordability is also a key consideration when it comes to meeting singles’ housing needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While first-timers can access various financial support grants from the age of 21 to aid in their purchase of a flat, this is, at this point, not available to singles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That said, I recognise that single buyers, too, have access to housing grants and can buy smaller BTO units in non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should the eligibility age be reduced, I believe singles can avail themselves of such grants, too, thus supportive of singles’ home affordability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the Government has budgetary concerns or believe that younger singles should not be incentivised to buy a place of their own, the level of housing grants accorded can be on a graduated scale, where grants provided for 28-year-olds are at a discount to the full enhanced CPF housing grants, with an annual step-up to the current eligible age of 35.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, singles aged below 35 who wish to have a place of their own today would have to either purchase a private residential property, which, needless to say, is significantly more expensive than public housing, or rent a flat in the open market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, even in the HDB rental market, many singles would be priced out of the market if they wish to rent a place of their own.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Median rents for a 3-room HDB flat are, currently, about S$2,000 a month, which is, essentially, the entire take-home salary of a Polytechnic graduate today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The purchase of a BTO 2-room flexi flat, on the other hand, is a lot more affordable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, while it is abundantly clear that many Singaporeans who may be single for various reasons before the age of 35 would like to have a place of their own, many simply cannot afford to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should we not look into further enabling single Singaporeans to meet their housing needs and aspirations?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The change in policy came about in 1991 by allowing singles over 35 to buy resale HDB flats but limited to 3-room flats in selected locations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The rules were further relaxed over the years, but the next big break came in 2013 when singles over 35 were, for the first time, allowed to buy new, subsidised 2-room flats directly from HDB.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, Minister for National Development Desmond Lee recently reassured Singaporeans that the Government cares about housing for singles, when he said at the Singapore Economic Policy Forum on 29 October 2021: “Some Singaporeans remain single for a variety of reasons, including obligation to family and parents, or a matter of choice, or a matter of life course.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But many still want or need their own living space.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They may wonder if we care about their housing needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To these Singaporeans, let me assure you: we do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We recognise your needs, your aspirations and your sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That’s why we’ve in fact been expanding housing options and grants for singles over the years.” However, 30 years on from the introduction of the Single Singapore Citizen scheme, singles below 35 remain largely precluded from owning their own HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there have recently been welcome exceptions carved out for certain special situations, such as for single parents, the general threshold of excluding singles below 35 years of age seems to have been retained by default since 1991, despite changing demographics and societal mindsets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This rule has serious implications on the growing number of singles under 35, depriving them of the security of home ownership if they are priced out of the private market, the private and HDB rental market and not having a place to call their own and build their own lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, current policy signals to single Singaporeans that their marital status, whether by choice or due to factors beyond their control, is somehow viewed as undesirable and undeserving of Government support for home ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this traditional life progression might have been more relevant back in 1991, we know now that Singaporeans are staying single for longer for myriad reasons and not necessarily moving straight from their parents’ home into a matrimonial home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Contrary to popular belief that the younger generation are eschewing marriage, surveys have shown that many single Singaporeans still want to get married.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, over the last 20 years, the general marriage rates for resident males and females have been consistent at 43.3 for males and 40.2 for females.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The latest data point on general marriage rates in 2021 is even higher on a year-on-year basis for both males and females, at 45.3 and 44.2, respectively.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What has changed is that Singaporeans are staying single for longer and getting married later in life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A 2013 survey conducted by IPS sheds some light on why Singaporeans are getting married later in life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The IPS found that, among respondents who wanted to get married, the key reasons for their getting married later in life than their ideal age were “the delayed acquisition of the markers of adulthood” and “not having a suitable partner.” At the same time, data shows that more young people are moving out of their parents’ home even before marriage.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There are, of course, those who are neither living with their parents nor living alone.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But there are also a considerable number who, while still living with their families, do not have the financial ability to live on their own, as much as they desire to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While it can be argued that some singles might have needed to move out given working from home requirements during the pandemic, many others have expressed a yearning simply to lead more independent lives in their early adulthood.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The data and trends highlight the negative effects of excluding those under the age of 35 from owning HDB flats and, considering these developments, it behoves the Government to revisit the issue and assess the validity of the main arguments against HDB flat ownership by singles under 35.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To this point, I am comforted by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s comments during the National Day Rally earlier this year, where he shared that, and I quote, “We have done our studies and planning.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We will have enough space for future generations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our problem is not finding the space to build enough flats, nor keeping homes affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We know how to do that.” Putting the issue of land scarcity aside, I would like to make three points on the issue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, data from past BTO exercises shows clearly singles do not compete with young couples and families for the same type of flats in non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The data shows that young married couples overwhelmingly apply for 3-room or larger BTO flats and very few apply for 2-room flats, whereas singles are limited to buying only 2-room flexi BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, first-timer singles can only apply for 2-room Flexi flats in non-mature locations, with a cap of 65% of the balance 60% of such flats meant for non-elderly applicants; in other words, at most, 39% of such flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This shows that even without making any adjustments to the unit mix of various types of flats, lowering the minimum age threshold for singles to buy a BTO flat from 35 to 28 is expected to have a minimal impact on young couples’ likelihood of securing a flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having said that, providing support for young couples and families should not be viewed as mutually exclusive from expanding HDB options for singles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the Government can loosen the BTO eligibility criteria for singles without in any way impinging on the subsidies and other benefits given to young couples, which may even be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, even if there were to be a question on the allocation of limited resources, such an exercise will always be a balancing act conducted in accordance with Government priorities and, more importantly, guided by fundamental principles and values.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our current policy measures have been described as imposing “anti-single penalties” and which, unknowingly, become signals to singles that their marital status, whether by their own volition or not, is viewed as undesirable and undeserving of Government support for home ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The next key argument against singles owning HDB flats is that it is somehow in conflict with the Government’s goals of encouraging marriage and family formation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If this hypothesis were true, then we might see an immediate dip in marriage rates for singles over 35 years old who have been able to buy an HDB flat of their own.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To test this, we looked at the number of marriages in the 35- to 39-year-old age group at two key points in time when HDB options for singles were expanded: after October 1991 when the Single Singapore Citizen scheme was first introduced; and after July 2013 when singles were allowed to buy 2-room BTO flats in non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The data showed that in the three-year period from 1992 to 1994, as well as from 2014 to 2016, marriage rates and the number of marriages for both males and females in the 35- to 39-year-old age group went up instead of falling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We accept that this could be a simple coincidence of timing between housing policy and marriage rates, which are, of course, affected by multiple factors and do not necessarily imply causation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the data does suggest that we need not be too circumspect about expanding HDB options for singles as a factor that will single-handedly cause a further delay or decline in marriages.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the contrary, allowing singles to have a home of their own might even encourage marriage and family formation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As elected Members of Parliament, we are given a mandate from and by the people we serve.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We, therefore, must lend a listening ear to the generation ahead of us and ensure that our public housing policies are both inclusive and reflective of the diversity of our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, almost nine in 10 Singaporeans own a flat – one of the highest home ownership rates in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: At the same time, we are keenly aware that housing preferences and aspirations change over time and across different life stages of families and individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Therefore, MND and HDB have been actively engaging Singaporeans to understand their needs and aspirations, as also reflected in Mr Louis Chua's theme for the Adjournment Motion – "housing needs for Singaporeans".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And we have been listening to Singaporeans, hearing their views and taking in their suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Most recently, as part of the year-long Long-Term Plan Review (LTPR), we have heard from over 15,000 people from all walks of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors shared with us that they would like to age-in-place in the neighbourhood that they are familiar with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Working adults shared with us that they would like to have workplaces closer to home to minimise commute and to have the flexibility to reconfigure their flats to provide more space as more of them work from home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Couples with young children told with us they would like to live near their family so that grandchildren can be taken care of by their grandparents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Young couples wanting to get married and settle down shared with us their anxieties of getting a flat at an affordable price, especially in a bullish property market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Singles, especially those older singles, shared with us that they would like to get a place of their own near their ageing parents so that they can better care for their elderly parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Younger Singaporeans have also shared with us that they value their own personal space and would like to stay by themselves, even if it is rental, on a temporary basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Many of them still wish to own their homes eventually.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We take them seriously and feed them into our Long-Term Plan Review, which was recently launched and exhibited at the URA Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We have received many valuable feedback and suggestions, some of which are quite similar to what Mr Louis Chua has raised today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are studying those suggestions carefully and we are engaging Singaporeans as part of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We would want to meet the needs of all Singaporeans, their aspirations and their wants if we can.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: But we have limited land and resources and would have to prioritise and allocate within these constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, I thank Mr Louis Chua for recognising these constraints and recognising the very difficult stresses and strains the Government has to deal with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: That is why we need to prioritise public housing for those who have more urgent housing needs, for example, implementing income eligibility criteria for BTO for married couples as well as for singles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Before that, I would like to assure Singaporeans that even as we engage all of you as part of the Forward Singapore exercise, we have already taken steps to address the concerns raised by various demographic groups and various segments of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are closely monitoring the situation, to assess if other measures are needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: On young couples, which Mr Louis Chua talked about, I am glad that Mr Louis Chua has recognised the many moves and steps that we have taken in terms of giving first-time couples priority, including in this recent August BTO launch as well as stepping up and enhancing the various grants and support that we give to first-time couples.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Louis Chua spoke about the demand for BTO flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Although the application numbers have risen and increased, four in 10 of the applicants did not choose a flat when invited to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are monitoring the supply situation, application rates and the locations where application rates are elevated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In terms of affordability, I would like to assure Singaporeans that this is an important consideration for HDB and the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Most first-timers only need to use less than a quarter of their monthly income to pay for their loan instalments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In fact, most of them can service their housing loans using their monthly CPF contributions, with little or no cash outlay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: He talked about singles and the need to cater to their needs, aspirations and wants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I am glad that Mr Louis Chua has also recognised that, over the years, the Government has been trying to accommodate and support their needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: More recently, we have also made changes to the BTO allocation quota.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In 2013, we opened access for singles to purchase new 2-room flats from HDB under the Single Singapore Citizen (SSC) scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We have also raised the allocation quota for these 2-room flats in 2015, from 30% to 50% of the non-senior quota in the non-mature estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And because we still see a fairly strong broad-based increase in housing demand across all groups, including singles, which Mr Louis Chua spoke about, we have further increased the quotas to better support all first-timers, including singles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: There is a vibrant rental market, with a wide variety of both public and private options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Some of these are provided by seniors or families who are renting out their rooms or flats to supplement their income and retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These spaces are attractive as they provide the flexibility of shorter-term rental contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Some even provide housekeeping services and fully furnished rooms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We see many commercial providers stepping up with innovative offerings that cater to the diverse range of needs for singles and youths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I think this shows that the market is functioning and responding agilely to consumer demand and preferences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is an important part of the entire housing market.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are looking at it and, certainly, many Singaporeans have also suggested this idea of lowering the age limit and eligibility criterion as part of our long-term plan review conversations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, these are considerations that we have to bear in mind.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is certainly something that we will continue to work towards as part of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will engage Singaporeans on their housing needs and aspirations and discuss how we can each play our part to build an inclusive home for our families and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Singaporeans' housing needs will become more diverse as our society becomes more diverse.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And housing is so much a core part of families, society and the social compact between the Government and our citizens, between each of us in society and across generations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Minister Desmond Lee will be launching our Forward Singapore engagements later this month and we hope that everyone will participate actively, giving us ideas, suggestions and co-develop these solutions together but, importantly, co-create solutions that bring Singapore together and bring Singapore forward, while balancing the needs of various groups of people for housing aspirations.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I adjourn the House pursuant to the Standing Order.
